title: Spend the view’s one red on the point the title names.
rule: Rule 05.3 gives each view one working red. In a chart, the red goes to the point, bar or line the title names, inside Rule 05.5’s keyline and with its own label, and every other mark takes the light fill on Newsprint and the context ink on Charcoal (Rule 05.7).

A line or a bar is one mark, and a run of columns is a set of marks, so a title can give one column of a run the red, as on Rule 14.12’s plate. A mark the title names only to measure the finding against, as “more than twice Zion’s” does on this rule’s plate, keeps the light fill with its label.

When a diagram or a map answers with its whole path or pattern, its title names no single mark. In a process, the path the reader’s question follows takes Charcoal at the subject weight, as on Rule 14.96’s diagram. A map gives the red only to a place its title names as a point, such as the town on Rule 14.118’s locator.

The named mark gives up the red and takes Charcoal at the subject weight when an error or a step the reader can take holds the red first (Rule 05.3), or when a reader would tie the mark to a party, since red there reads as a party’s color (Rules 01.1, 01.2 and 14.7).

Rule 05.1 keeps the red within 5 percent of the drawing at every width, so a named area, whose size follows its data, takes Charcoal at any size, and so does a named mark that would pass that share, such as a tall column in a short run.

text: One red mark tells a reader where to look first, and the title tells them why. A second red mark splits their attention, and red that codes a group reads as a warning about that group.
why.basis: Design judgment, from the chart system our founder and editor approved in November 2026

builders: Name the one point in the spec’s labels.point, which draws it in red with its keyline and every other mark in the light fill; where the subject ink takes its place, labels.named does it instead, with a list for two marks, and a diagram or map that names no mark sets neither. The kit counts working reds and fails a view whose red falls on two jobs or covers more than 5 percent of the drawing at any width it checks.

specs.label: The point
specs.value: Pillar Red with a 1 px Charcoal keyline (Rule 05.5)

specs.label: Its label
specs.value: Beside the mark, in the text ink

specs.label: Marks named together
specs.value: Share the red, as the bars of one age band do

specs.label: A chart of one mark
specs.value: One line, bar or path, with no other mark to set it apart from, in Charcoal at the subject weight, the title’s value labeled

specs.label: A diagram’s path
specs.value: The path the question follows in Charcoal at the subject weight and the branches it leaves in the context ink; where the reader’s own case picks the path, as in a decision tree, every branch in one ink; no red

specs.label: A comparison
specs.value: The light fill, with its label

specs.label: An error, a step or a sign
specs.value: Charcoal at the subject weight, with the label

specs.label: A party tie
specs.value: A state, a Congress or chamber whose majority readers know, an election result, money spent to elect a candidate, or a policy readers link to one party: Charcoal at the subject weight, with the label

specs.label: Two findings
specs.value: Both in Charcoal at the subject weight, each with its label

specs.label: A named area, or past 5 percent of the drawing
specs.value: Charcoal, with the label (Rule 05.1): a part of a treemap, pie, donut or funnel, a region on a map, a node (a box or dot where a diagram’s links meet), a cell of a matrix, or a line or band whose width carries an amount, such as a flow

specs.label: A total or national line
specs.value: Dashed in the text’s ink, with its own label

specs.label: A total or national figure elsewhere
specs.value: As a point, an open ring; in a list, the first row, set apart; on a map, beside it with its name and value, outside every region

specs.label: Red never
specs.value: Codes a series, a group, a step on a scale or in a process, or a sign, such as a deficit or a loss

correct.caption: The title names Great Smoky Mountains, and its bar alone takes the view’s red, inside its keyline. Zion, which the title names only to compare, stays gray with its value like every other park.
correct.alt: One red bar, the one the title names, and every other park in gray. Great Smoky Mountains National Park drew 11.5 million recreation visits in 2025, the most of the 63 national parks and more than twice Zion’s 5.0 million.
correct.notes: The kit draws it from the research lead's frozen National Park Service counts, the 12 most visited parks.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 14.6. Red falls on three parks while the title names one, so a reader cannot tell which bar the title means.
failure.alt: Failure case: do not publish. The same bars with three parks in red, Great Smoky Mountains, Zion and Yellowstone, under a title that names one.

examples.example: Recreation visits, the 12 most visited national parks, 2025
